title: Morrow Micro Decision — Complete Overview
body:
The Morrow Micro Decision is a home computer record of the 1982–1985 era, originating with Morrow Designs.

The 'wise' CP/M machine: Z80, 64K, bundled software, $1,195 — the thinking buyer's choice. George Morrow's S-100 roots showed; the MD series were solid citizens. The Pivot (1985) was an early DOS laptop.

Notable examples include Micro Decision MD2/MD3 (1982). This record is the front door of the database: start here, then follow the teaching ladder from the simple definition (record 2) through the engineering deep-dives (records 4–6) to the advanced restoration and collecting guides.

title: What Is Morrow Micro Decision? — Definition
body:
Home computers are the affordable microcomputers of roughly 1975–1995 that put programmable machines on desks and in living rooms: Altair and Apple I kits, the 1977 trinity (Apple II, TRS-80, PET), 1980s 8-bit classics (Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Atari 800, BBC Micro), 16-bit powerhouses (Amiga, Atari ST), and the IBM PC compatibles that eventually absorbed the market. They were programmed in BASIC, expanded with cartridges and floppy drives, and taught a generation to code.

In the context of this database, the Morrow Micro Decision is presented as one home computer record among the home computers family. The 'wise' CP/M machine: Z80, 64K, bundled software, $1,195 — the thinking buyer's choice.

title: Origins and History of Morrow Micro Decision
body:
The Morrow Micro Decision belongs to the 1982–1985 era and traces to Morrow Designs.

The MITS Altair 8800 (1975, $439 kit) ignited the microcomputer revolution; Microsoft's first product was Altair BASIC. 1977's trinity — Apple II, Commodore PET, TRS-80 — made computers retail products. Atari and Commodore's price wars drove 8-bit machines into millions of homes; the Commodore 64 (1982) became the best-selling computer model ever (~17 million). Sinclair's ZX Spectrum (1982) put Britain's bedrooms in code; the BBC Micro (1981) put computers in every British school. The Amiga (1985) and Atari ST (1985) brought multitasking, MIDI, and near-arcade graphics. IBM's PC (1981) with its open architecture invited clones; by the early 1990s the PC compatible had won, and the home-computer era closed as Windows 95 unified the market.

Within that longer story, Morrow Micro Decision: George Morrow's S-100 roots showed; the MD series were solid citizens. The Pivot (1985) was an early DOS laptop.

title: How Morrow Micro Decision Works
body:
An 8-bit CPU (MOS 6502, Zilog Z80, Motorola 6809) fetched BASIC or machine code from ROM, ran programs in tens of kilobytes of RAM, and drew text and chunky graphics to a TV via a video chip (VIC-II, ANTIC/GTIA, ULA). Sound came from chips like the SID or AY-3-8910. Storage was cassette tape (slow, cheap) then 5.25-inch floppies; cartridges gave instant games. Users typed BASIC programs from magazines, saved to tape, and learned computing by doing — no hard drive, no internet, just the machine and its manual.

Applied to the Morrow Micro Decision (1982–1985, Morrow Designs): The Pivot (1985) was an early DOS laptop.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Morrow Micro Decision — Components
body:
Every Morrow Micro Decision is an assembly of the home computers family's standard parts:

• CPU — 6502, Z80, 6809, 68000 — the 8/16-bit brains.
• Video chip — VIC-II, ANTIC, ULA, Denise — sprites, scrolling, color.
• Sound chip — SID 6581, AY-3-8910, POKEY — chiptune voices.
• RAM — 4K to 512K typical; bank switching stretched it.
• ROM BASIC — Built-in BASIC interpreter in ROM — instant programming.
• Cassette interface — Kansas City standard tones; 300–2000 baud saves.
• Floppy drive — 1541, 810, 3-inch — DOS on a disk.
• Cartridge port — Instant-load ROM games and expansions.
• Joystick ports — Atari-standard 9-pin; the social interface.
• Expansion bus — User port, cartridge, or PDS slots for hardware hackers.

When examining a surviving Morrow Micro Decision, identify these parts in order: CPU, Video chip, Sound chip, RAM, ROM BASIC, Cassette interface.

title: Key Figures Behind Home Computers
body:
The people who made home computers possible:

• Steve Wozniak — Apple I/II designer; the hacker's hacker.
• Jack Tramiel — 'Business is war'; Commodore's price-war general.
• Clive Sinclair — ZX80/81/Spectrum; cheap computers for the masses.
• Jay Miner — Atari 400/800 and Amiga chip designer; 'father of the Amiga'.
• Chuck Peddle — MOS 6502 creator; the $25 CPU that made it affordable.
• Federico Faggin — Z80 architect after the 8080; the other 8-bit pillar.
• Sophie Wilson & Steve Furber — BBC Micro designers; later ARM's creators.
• Bill Gates & Paul Allen — Altair BASIC (1975); Microsoft's founding product.

title: Home Computers Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of home computers:

• BASIC — Beginners' All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code; the lingua franca of home computing.
• PEEK/POKE — Reading/writing memory directly — hardware control from BASIC.
• sprite — Hardware-moved graphic object; the VIC-II had 8.
• raster interrupt — Retiming the video chip mid-frame for split screens and effects.
• copper — Amiga co-processor that rewrote video registers per scanline.
• blitter — Amiga block-image transferrer; fast graphics moves in hardware.
• bank switching — Paging RAM/ROM in 64K chunks to exceed address limits.
• fast loader — Third-party floppy speed-ups (e.g., Epyx FastLoad) replacing miserable stock DOS.
• cracktro — Demo-scene intro on cracked games; an art form.
• demoscene — Programmers pushing hardware limits for art's sake; still alive.
• GOTO — Dijkstra's enemy; the structural unit of spaghetti BASIC.
• load "$" ,8,1 — The Commodore incantation every C64 kid memorized.

title: Morrow Micro Decision in Culture
body:
Home computers were the bedrooms and basements where a generation learned to think in code. Magazine type-ins, playground cassette swaps, the demoscene's impossible effects, BBS numbers scribbled in notebooks — a folk culture of computing before the internet. The Commodore 64's SID chip is still sampled; chiptune is a genre. 'Press Play on Tape' is a Proustian trigger for millions.

The Morrow Micro Decision carries that cultural charge directly: The Pivot (1985) was an early DOS laptop.

title: Collecting and Preserving Morrow Micro Decision
body:
C64s, Spectrums, and Amigas are plentiful but yellowing (retrobright carefully, or embrace it). Recap power supplies and disk drives before use — RIFA filter caps crack and smoke. Original boxes and manuals multiply value. CRT monitors are the fragile part; modern scalers (OSSC, RetroTINK) bridge to LCDs. Socketed chips (SID, CIA) are theft/loss targets — inventory them.

For the Morrow Micro Decision specifically: The 'wise' CP/M machine: Z80, 64K, bundled software, $1,195 — the thinking buyer's choice.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working Morrow Micro Decision with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: Morrow Micro Decision Restoration Guide
body:
Recap PSUs first (RIFA X2 caps fail spectacularly). Clean edge connectors and cartridge ports with isopropyl. Replace drive belts in floppy drives; align heads only with proper disks. Check for battery leakage (Amiga A4000, some PC boards) — neutralize and repair traces. Keep machines dry, cool, and out of attics.

Restoration order for a Morrow Micro Decision: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical home computer record without a current-limited bring-up.
